specPoints.text: use the left-hand rule to predict the direction of the resulting force when a wire carries a current perpendicular to a magnetic field

primer.text: Three directions, one hand: the first finger along the field, the second along the current, and the thumb fires out the force. This note drills Fleming's left-hand rule for wires crossing a magnetic field — including the conventional-current trap and what happens when either input flips.

lessons.title: Predicting the force with Fleming's left-hand rule
lessons.opening: The left-hand rule turns three directions into one prediction: first finger along the magnetic field, second finger along the current, and the thumb at right angles to both gives the direction of the force on the wire. It works whenever the current runs perpendicular to the field — the geometry the rule was built for.
keyPoints: The first finger points along the magnetic field, from north to south.
The second finger points along the conventional current in the wire.
The thumb then gives the direction of the force on the wire.
The three fingers are held at right angles to each other in a left hand.
The rule predicts the force when the current is perpendicular to the field.

low.restatement: Hold the left hand flat: point the first finger the way the field runs, the second finger the way the current flows, and the thumb sticks out in the direction the wire gets pushed.
low.analogy: It is a three-arrow machine: feed in field and current, and the thumb fires out the answer.
low.examPointer: Name the fingers in order — first (field), second (current), thumb (force) — examiners check the mapping, not just the pose.

medium.restatement: The rule encodes the perpendicular geometry of the motor effect: force, field and current are mutually at right angles, so a left-hand coordinate frame fixes the third direction once two are known. The rule applies to the conventional-current direction, so electron flow runs against the second finger, and it presumes the current crosses the field — parallel arrangements fall outside it.
medium.analogy: Like a 3D jigsaw: two pieces click in, and the shape of the frame forces the third piece into one place only.
medium.examPointer: Check the current direction in the diagram first — using electron flow instead of conventional current is the classic inversion error.

check.stem: Which finger of the left hand gives the direction of the FORCE?

options.explanation: First finger field, second finger current, thumb force.
The first finger carries the field direction.
The second finger carries the current direction.
The palm plays no role in the rule.

check.stem: The FIRST finger in Fleming's left-hand rule points along:

options.text: the magnetic field, north to south
options.explanation: Field is assigned to the first finger.
Current belongs to the second finger.
Force belongs to the thumb.
Electron flow runs opposite to the conventional current.

check.stem: A wire carries current at right angles to a field. The rule predicts the force direction. What is assumed about the current used in the rule?

options.text: the conventional current, from positive to negative
options.explanation: The rule uses conventional current, not electron flow.
Electrons run against the second finger.
Direction, not magnitude, is what the rule needs.
There is no separate 'resistance current'.

check.stem: The current in the wire is reversed while the field stays fixed. What does the rule now predict?

options.text: a force in the opposite direction
options.explanation: Reversing one input mirrors the predicted force.
The prediction flips with the current.

options.text: a larger force in the same direction
options.explanation: Reversal changes direction, not size.
The wire still crosses the field, so a force remains.

check.stem: Which arrangement is NOT the perpendicular case that the rule predicts?

options.text: a wire carrying current parallel to the field lines
options.explanation: The rule predicts forces for currents perpendicular to the field.

options.text: a wire carrying current across the field
options.explanation: That is exactly the case the rule covers.

options.text: a wire between two opposite poles
options.explanation: The gap field is a standard case for the rule.

options.text: a straight wire rather than a coil
options.explanation: The rule works wire by wire, straight or coiled.

check.stem: State what each of the three fingers represents in the left-hand rule.
check.modelAnswer: First finger along the magnetic field, second finger along the current, thumb along the force.

check.stem: State which hand is used in the rule for motor-effect force prediction.
check.modelAnswer: The left hand is used for predicting the force in the motor effect.

check.stem: Explain why reversing the field direction flips the predicted force.
check.modelAnswer: The three directions form a right-angled set: with the current unchanged, pointing the first finger the opposite way leaves the thumb pointing the opposite way too. The geometry of the hand mirrors the physics — the force depends on both inputs, so flipping either flips the result.

check.stem: A horizontal wire runs north, carrying current northwards, in a field directed from east to west. Predict the initial force direction using the rule.
check.modelAnswer: First finger points west (field), second finger points north (current), and the left-hand thumb then points vertically upwards — the wire is pushed up out of its position.

glossary.definition: The rule assigning field to the first finger, current to the second and force to the thumb of a left hand.
The direction of current flow from positive to negative, used by the rule.
The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field, whose direction the rule predicts.

workedExample.prompt: A current-carrying wire is placed into the magnetic field between the poles of a magnet, as shown in the diagram. Use Fleming's left-hand rule to determine the direction of the force on the wire.
steps: Read the current direction along the wire from the diagram.
Read the field direction between the poles, from north to south.
Align the first finger with the field and the second finger with the current.
The thumb then gives the force direction; from the diagram this is vertically downwards.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The force on the wire acts vertically downwards, as given by the thumb of the left hand with first finger along the field and second finger along the current.
